ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Establishes Six-Month Caretaker Administration in Tigray
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Establishes Six-Month Caretaker Administration in Tigray - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Establishes Six-Month Caretaker Administration in Tigray Million Hailesilassie / Deutsche Welle The regional capital Mekele in Tigray (file photo). 16 October 2026 The Reporter (Addis Ababa) By Bruck Getachew New admin tasked with restoring security, rebuilding institutions and preparing for elections Ethiopia's federal government has established a six-month caretaker administration for the Tigray region, assigning it responsibility for restoring security, rebuilding damaged infrastructure and organizing elections intended to return the region to an elected government. The Council of Ministers established the administration under a regulation following a decision by the House of Federation, which cited Article 62(9) of the Constitution and Article 14(2)(b) of Proclamation No. 359/1995 as the legal basis for establishing an interim administration in the region. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The government said repeated efforts to resolve the conflict in Tigray under the Pretoria peace agreement had failed, blaming the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) for obstructing implementation. It also accused the TPLF leadership of initiating renewed fighting, which it described as the group's fourth failed attempt to wage war. The government said the new administration was intended to help Tigray emerge from prolonged conflict, restore peace and enable residents to exercise self-government and benefit from development. From The Reporter Magazine Drought Emergency or Seasonal Deficit ? Published on 2026-09-02 By The Reporter Magazine What the Old Developmental State Got Wrong Published on 2026-10-02 By Samson Berhane 25-Year Sentences & Retroactive Laws: Controversial Draft Law Sparks Fears of Growing Authoritarianism in Tigray Published on 2026-06-21 By Yared Nigussie Red Sea Rivalries: What a Shifting Geopolitical Landscape Means for Ethiopia and The Horn Published on 2026-08-31 By Yared Nigussie Under its mandate, the caretaker administration will work to restore stability, rebuild government institutions and damaged infrastructure, resume interrupted social services and facilitate the return of displaced residents to their homes. It will also coordinate with federal defense, police and security institutions, as well as regional security forces, to establish stability across the region, including at the local administrative level. Its responsibilities include facilitating the disarmament and reintegration of armed groups and restructuring the region's security apparatus. A central objective is to establish conditions for free and transparent elections within six months, allowing Tigray to resume its place as a regular component of Ethiopia's federal system under an elected government. The administration will also coordinate media activities, organize public forums and undertake measures intended to promote reconciliation, rebuild public confidence and prepare residents for reconstruction and development. The government said the caretaker administration must base its activities on Ethiopia's national interests and territorial integrity, as well as the fundamental interests of the people of Tigray. Its authority will be limited to providing routine regional services and creating conditions for the next election. It will not undertake matters with longer-term strategic implications, the government said, and will operate under the direction and supervision of the federal government. The administration's senior officials are Asefa Abraha Hagos, chief executive for administration and public services; Tewodros Aregay Woldeselassie (PhD), chief executive for the economy and reconstruction; Gebre Egziabher Beyene Hailu (Brig. Gen.), chief executive for security and peace; and Redae Hailuom Woldeselassie, chief executive for political affairs and public organization. Shishay Amare (PhD) was appointed mayor of Mekele, the regional capital. The federal government will provide direction, support and oversight for the officials' activities, according to the announcement. Read the original article on Reporter . ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia has established a six-month caretaker administration in the Tigray region, aimed at restoring security, rebuilding infrastructure, and preparing for elections to reinstate an elected government. This decision follows the federal government's assertion that previous efforts to resolve the conflict under the Pretoria peace agreement were unsuccessful, with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) being blamed for obstructing progress and initiating renewed fighting. The caretaker administration will focus on stabilizing the region, resuming social services, and facilitating the return of displaced residents. It will also oversee disarmament and the restructuring of security forces, operating under the federal government's direction. Key officials have been appointed to lead various sectors, including administration, economy, security, and political affairs, with the goal of creating conditions for free and transparent elections within six months.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia, EU Reaffirm Commitment to Cooperation On Economic Progress, Regional Stability
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia, EU Reaffirm Commitment to Cooperation On Economic Progress, Regional Stability - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia, EU Reaffirm Commitment to Cooperation On Economic Progress, Regional Stability 16 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — The Ethiopian delegation met with European Commissioner for International Partnerships Commissioner Jozef Síkela on the sidelines of the ongoing IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings. The discussions focused on Ethiopia's economic progress, the situation in the country's northern regions, and opportunities to strengthen alignment on development priorities and sustain cooperation between Ethiopia and the European Union (EU). Commissioner Síkela reaffirmed the EU's strong political commitment to Ethiopia, recognizing the country as a critical stabilizing anchor and reliable partner in the Horn of Africa, particularly in the Red Sea region, amid persistent fragility and evolving regional challenges. He also reiterated the EU's continued support for Ethiopia's stability and development, underscoring its strategic role in promoting regional stability and cooperation. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia and the European Union (EU) have reaffirmed their commitment to enhancing cooperation on economic development and regional stability during a meeting on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings. Ethiopian officials engaged with European Commissioner for International Partnerships, Jozef Síkela, discussing Ethiopia's economic progress and the situation in its northern regions. Síkela emphasized the EU's strong political commitment to Ethiopia, recognizing its role as a stabilizing force in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region amidst ongoing challenges. He reiterated the EU's support for Ethiopia's stability and development, highlighting the importance of collaboration in promoting regional stability.

ethiopia.title: From Sinai to the Nile - Egypt Cannot Demand Peace From Israel While Threatening War Against Ethiopia
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: From Sinai to the Nile - Egypt Cannot Demand Peace From Israel While Threatening War Against Ethiopia - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: From Sinai to the Nile - Egypt Cannot Demand Peace From Israel While Threatening War Against Ethiopia 16 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) By Professor Al Mariam On October 14, 2026, President Abdel Fatah El-Sisi responded to warnings made by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich that Egypt would lose its Sinai Peninsula should it attack Israel. El-Sisi asserted that his country had struggled for its land, that it had no plans to annex any territory and that it wanted only security and stability. El-Sisi's staternent is based on the sound diplornatic principle that states do not have to threaten the sovereignty and territorial integrity of another country in order to defend their own interests, territorial integrity, and security. Ethiopia has never made threats of any kind to occupy or attack Egyptian territory. The building and operation of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) in the Blue Nile is a development project in Ethiopia completed in September 2025 with the blood sweat and tears of Ethiopians. The controversy over the GERD is simply about filling and operating the dam, water security downstream, and lack of a shared agreement for cooperation--not Ethiopia's claim over any Egyptian territory. Ethiopia has never denied Egypt's right to the waters of the Nile River under international law. Ethiopia also has an unquestioned sovereign right to develop its water resources and produce hydroelectric power for its economy consistent with the 1997 UN Watercourses Convention, which mandates riparian countries to make equitable and reasonable use of shared water resources and cause no significant harm in doing so. In much the same way as El Sisi communicated to Israel, he should send a similar message of peaceful coexistence to Ethiopia: "Egypt does not want war with Ethiopia. Egypt has no territorial designs on Ethiopia. Egypt respects the sovereignty of Ethiopia, and it expects the same from Ethiopia. Egypt does not and will not support any terror groups or countries that sponsor terror groups to commit terrorism in Ethiopia, covertly provide them with arms and other military equipment under cover of night or otherwise. Differences between the two countries must be settled through negotiations, international law, technological cooperation, and security assurances to each other." Indeed, this is the standard by which Egypt must deal with Israel, Ethiopia, and all other countries in the Horn of Africa. Three principles in President El-Sisi's statement should be highlighted. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn First, he believes that Sinai belongs to Egypt and that its territorial integrity should be preserved. Second, he affirms Egypt wants to defend its territory, not to annex someone else's land. Third, Egypt's national security does not need to compromise the sovereignty of some other state. These three principles apply equally to Ethiopia. Egypt cannot reasonably insist that lsrael respect Egyptian territory while treating Ethiopia's developrnent of a darn on Ethiopian territory as a threat that justifies coercive rnilitary action. Ethiopia has publicly declared tirne and again that is prepared to accornrnodate legitirnate Egyptian concerns about downstrearn water security through peaceful negotiation in the spirit of brotherhood, rnutual respect and binding legal arrangernents that protect the legitirnate interests of Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt. Ethiopia does not deny Nile waters are essential to Egyptian agriculture, drinking-water supply, industry, and national economy. The fact remains Egypt is heavily dependent on the Nile River, while Ethiopia is the principal source of the Blue Nile's headwaters; 86 percent of Nile waters originate in Ethiopia. Egypt's security concerns do not confer a veto over Ethiopia's development. These geographical facts establish a shared need for economic cooperation, not an exclusive right for Egypt to determine how Ethiopia develops its water resources. GERD is Ethiopia's source of energy to produce electricity and propel its economic development. The major concern that the GERD can impact the scheduling of the water discharge from its reservoir during drought periods can be addressed in a transparent process of information exchange, coordinated operation of the dam, rigorous dam safety regime, and joint drought management system. In January 2020, in a joint statement by Egypt, Ethiopia, Sudan, the United States, and the World Bank, certain areas of agreement were defined, including the staged filling of the reservoir, drought management, the long-term operation of the dam, coordination, information exchange, and dispute resolution. The problern has been irnplernentation. Egypt has been a rnajor irnpedirnent in the process. Egypt is obsessively fixed on a sharne and blarne garne against Ethiopia and stuck to the antiquated colonial era agreernents. Hardly a week passes by without Egypt launching a rnedia dernonization carnpaign against Ethiopia. Egypt has used the rnantra of "unilateralisrn" against Ethiopia accusing it of neglecting the interests of the down-strearn countries, and violating international law and norrns. Ethiopia continues to stand firm in its commitment to assert its right to development and ensure that its rightful use of shared water resources is recognized. The Declaration of Principles 2015 between Egypt, Ethiopia, and Sudan and principles of international watercourse law provide a solution framework. The principles set forth by the Declaration and the Watercourses are that the waters of the Nile may be used in a just and reasonable manner through cooperation and due diligence not to cause any damage to other states. The important point is that the right to water security of the downstream state is not equivalent to an unlimited right to control upstream water resources. Neither can upstream sovereignty mean that the downstream consequences can just be disregarded. The way out of this deadlock is negotiation of rules that are practical, evidence-based, and reciprocal. Egyptian threats and rumors of war against Ethiopia over the Nile The argurnent that Egypt should adopt a peaceful doctrine toward Ethiopia is not based on speculation or guesswork. There is a long docurnented history of Egyptian rhetoric, warnings about rnilitary options, and regional rnilitary signaling surrounding the Nile dispute. The distinction between a threat, a policy staternent, and an actual decision to use force rnatters. The record dernonstrates why Ethiopia has reason to take Egypt's incessantly hostile rhetoric seriously. In 1979, President Anwar Sadat warned that Egypt would not passively accept a threat to its water supply. He dramatically declared, "If Ethiopia takes any action to block our right to the Nile water, there will be no alternative but for us to use force." In 2013, President Mohamed Morsi at a televised meeting proclaimed Egypt would support militant forces in Ethiopia and even attack the dam. Over the past seven years, President El-Sisi has warned that tampering with Egypt's Nile water security is its red line, and that the consequences would affect all of the region. Not to appear overly aggressive, El-Sisi has also been speaking with forked tongue that he would prefer diplomacy than not military force, and that Egypt acknowledges the right of Ethiopia to produce power, provided Egypt's water security remains intact. Using Egyptian military power against Ethiopia is not an option. The defeats that Egypt suffered when its forces invaded Ethiopia in the nineteenth century should serve as a lesson not to use military force. In the past, the Egyptian military has launched campaigns to increase Egyptian influence in the Horn of Africa, which includes the Red Sea and the Ethiopian Highlands. History teaches that using military action against Ethiopia will not make Egypt the dominant country or guarantee its exclusive use of Nile waters or solve disputes between the two countries for a lasting peace. The Khedive of Egypt, Ismail Pasha, undertook an invasion of the Ethiopian Empire through military means in the years 1874 and 1876 with the aim of taking control of the whole Nile River Basin to build an empire in Africa. In the Battle of Gundet (1875), Ethiopian forces crushed Egyptian forces. A well-known scholar observed, "Egyptian armies, often with European and American officers, were defeated and practically annihilated by Ethiopian forces led by the Emperor Yohannes on several occasions." In the Battle of Gura (1876), Ethiopian forces routed invading Egyptian forces. One scholar noted, "Gura, fought six months later [Gundet], confirms the superior capabilities of the Ethiopian military." Another noted, "Yohannes met the Egyptians in Hamasien and defeated them decisively at Gura in a three days' battle, 7-9 March 1876." In the Battle of Adwa against colonial Italy which took place on March 1, 1896, Ethiopian wiped out a highly armed modern European army within just a few hours. A highly regarded contemporary historian wrote, "Unlike Napoleon's Russian campaign, the Adwa campaign ended in victory. This is greatness." The historical lesson learned here is that Ethiopia cannot be considered as a country which would bow down to its enernies due to rnilitary superiority. Superior rnilitary equiprnent does not guarantee the achievernent of strategic objectives. The invasions launched by Egypt against Ethiopia in the nineteenth century did not succeed, and in any new war waged against Ethiopia, the result will be the sarne. It is not a stretch of the imagination to compare Israel's wars with Egypt's nineteenth-century campaigns against Ethiopia. During the June 1967 Six-Day War, Egypt was defeated by Israel and its Arab allies. The collapse of the Egyptian army took place in Sinai, and Israel captured the Sinai Peninsula. During the October War of 1973, Egypt won early victories in crossing the Suez Canal and penetrating the defenses of Israel in Sinai. Israel retaliated, crossed the Suez Canal and surrounded Egypt's Third Army. Sinai was finally reclaimed diplomatically by Egypt, after the signing of the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty, when Israel withdrew from Sinai in 1982. The strategic significance and political implications of this war is that it allowed Egypt to reclaim Sinai through diplomacy and the 1979 peace agreement. ln the dispute over the Nile, the lesson for Egypt is that its own history proves the usefulness of shifting frorn rnilitary confrontation to diplornatic resolution. Egypt won back Sinai through diplornacy and a peace agreernent after sorne rnilitary actions. Egypt does not need to be in a continuous state of war with lsrael. Military action against Ethiopia will neither lead to Egyptian domination over the Nile, ensure the safety of Egypt's water supply nor force Ethiopia to become a colonial/client state. Rather than threatening war and attacking Ethiopia, President El-Sisi should give a strong signal to Ethiopia and the Nile Basis countries about peaceful coexistence and prosperity through the fair use of Nile water. lndeed, Egypt should sign the Cornprehensive Frarnework Agreernent which establishes an institutional frarnework to coordinate basin-wide rnanagernent and developrnent of the Nile. The Nile River does not have to be an obstacle between Ethiopia and Egypt; rather, it should become the link between the two nations. Being united by many factors in common such as the history of the river and economics, the two nations should join hands to turn the Nile water into an engine of peace and prosperity. Ethiopia will never be threatened or intimidated militarily by Egypt in its lawful use of the Nile. Certainly, Ethiopia has no intention or desire to threaten or destabilize Egypt or use military means to dictate the way Egypt develops itself. The events involving Gundet and Gura show that Ethiopia will not be intimidated to give up its sovereignty. The events surrounding the Arab-Israeli war show that victory and defeat on the battlefield will not necessarily resolve the political problems involved. The return of Sinai shows the benefit of diplomacy and agreements. A true victory is one that preserves peace and the sovereignty of a nation. The history of Ethiopians indicates that they have always been strong and united in the defense of their homeland. Whether it was the Battle of Gundet and Gura or the Battle of Adwa, the Ethiopian people showed their capability of organizing their troops and using difficult terrains in order to repel their enemies. The defense of Ethiopia against the invasion of Somalia in 1977-1978 gives one more example of the ability of Ethiopian to resist and repel invaders. One lesson that can be learned from these battles is that when the sovereignty of Ethiopia has ever been challenged, then its people have always shown great determination, resilience and ability to defend their land. This glorious tradition is part of every Ethiopian, but the most important lesson that this tradition teaches us is that the greatest victory is that which is won without any battle. But if the battle becomes inevitable, then every Ethiopian is willing to fight for his motherland, making the Ethiopian National Defense Force invincible. What to do? Ethiopia, Egypt, and Sudan should commit to non-aggression -- pledging not to threaten or use force against one another in violation of the UN Charter, not to support terrorism against each other and to refrain from doing anything that destabilizes the region. The three countries should establish practical arrangements for sharing information, ensuring dam safety, mitigating drought risks, and coordinating reservoir operations. It is important to ensure Ethiopia's rights to manage its water resources fairly and reasonably, while taking into account the concerns of the downstream nations. Technical differences can be sorted out by negotiations and consultations. Moreover, regular military communications and dialogue under the guidance of the African Union should be held and issues addressed in good faith and good will. lf Egypt's clairn is that respect of territorial sovereignty rernoves the possibility of war, then Egypt ought to consider Ethiopia under sirnilar circurnstances. lf Egypt thinks that its security is best guaranteed by peaceful negotiations between itself and lsrael, then Ethiopia rnust be considered under sirnilar conditions. This should not be about Egypt losing or Ethiopia winning; it should be about reaching a solution where neither country is forced to choose between developrnent and security for its neighbor. Egyptian leaders should see the paradox -- the irony-- in rnaking a staternent saying it has no secret plan against lsrael when rnilitary threats are still part of the public discourse about the Ethiopian use of Nile waters. President El-Sisi has articulated a policy that is worth adhering to: Egypt does not need the land of any other country for its security. Ethiopia does not need Egypt to feel insecure in order to develop. The Nile should be rnanaged through cooperation, not coercion; through agreernent, not through threats; and through respect, not through historical anirnosities. This is the peace policy Egypt needs to apply to Ethiopia - and the test to which its rhetoric should be held. Let's join hands and ensure that we all prosper as countries within the Nile Basin and rnake each one of us NlLE GREAT! Read the original article on ENA . El-Sisi emphasized Egypt's commitment to its territorial integrity and security without threatening others. The article argues that Egypt cannot demand peace from Israel while simultaneously threatening Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), a project aimed at Ethiopia's economic development. Ethiopia has consistently stated it does not seek to occupy Egyptian territory and is willing to negotiate water security concerns. The piece highlights the importance of cooperation and mutual respect between Egypt and Ethiopia, advocating for diplomatic solutions rather than military threats, drawing on historical lessons from past conflicts. Ultimately, it calls for a framework that fosters shared management of Nile resources for the benefit of both nations.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Eyes Bigger Role in Africa's Investment, Financial Markets - House Speaker
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Eyes Bigger Role in Africa's Investment, Financial Markets - House Speaker - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Eyes Bigger Role in Africa's Investment, Financial Markets - House Speaker 16 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia is positioning itself as an increasingly important investment destination and financial market in Africa, driven by economic reforms and expanding cross-border investment partnerships, Speaker of the House of People's Representatives Ahmed Shide said. Addressing the Dangote Petroleum Refinery IPO Ethiopia Investor Roadshow, organized by the Ethiopian Securities Exchange (ESX) in collaboration with Dangote Industries Limited in Addis Ababa this afternoon, Ahmed said Ethiopia's economic reforms are opening new opportunities for domestic and international investors. The reforms are also strengthening Africa's capacity to finance its own development, the Speaker elaborated. "With an expanding economy, ongoing reforms, and a growing private sector, we envision Ethiopia becoming an increasingly important investment destination and financial market in Africa." Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines He highlighted the establishment of the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority, the Ethiopian Securities Exchange and supporting market infrastructure as key milestones in modernizing the country's financial system and mobilizing long-term capital. "Ethiopia's emerging capital market presents significant opportunities for domestic and international investors, financial institutions, and businesses," he said. Ahmed said the introduction of Dangote Petroleum Refinery's initial public offering to qualified Ethiopian investors demonstrates the growing potential for African businesses and investors to engage across national borders. The speaker further stressed that investor confidence, transparency, regulatory cooperation and robust investor protection are essential to building a credible and sustainable capital market, particularly as securities offerings increasingly cross-national borders. He expressed confidence that the country's expanding economy, ongoing reforms and growing private sector would strengthen its position in Africa's investment landscape, welcoming international businesses and financial institutions to participate in the transformation. "We welcome international businesses and financial institutions that wish to participate in this transformation and contribute to the development of our capital market." Addressing the occasion, Dangote Group President Aliko Dangote for his part has reaffirmed his commitment to expanding investments in Ethiopia. "Our investment in Ethiopia has no limit," he said, emphasizing the group's commitment to reinvesting its earnings locally and building a long-term partnership that supports the country's economic transformation. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's New Political Chapter - Sovereign Sea Access At the Heart of National Ambition
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's New Political Chapter - Sovereign Sea Access At the Heart of National Ambition - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's New Political Chapter - Sovereign Sea Access At the Heart of National Ambition 15 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Ethiopia's new five-year political chapter opens with a defining national ambition: building a peaceful, democratic and prosperous state while pursuing sovereign access to the sea. Under the Medemer Government, the government is highly anticipated to translating its electoral mandate into tangible improvements in citizens' lives while strengthening Ethiopia's strategic position in the Horn of Africa. At the heart of this agenda lies Ethiopia's sovereign sea access aspiration. As one of the world's most populous landlocked countries, Ethiopia has a compelling economic interest in reliable access to maritime trade. Securing such access through mutually beneficial arrangements could ease logistical constraints, improve export competitiveness, attract investment and deepen regional economic integration. Yet, maritime access is part of a broader national transformation. The success of Ethiopia's new political chapter will depend equally on consolidating peace, strengthening democratic institutions, advancing national reconciliation and building an inclusive economy. The Medemer philosophy, which emphasizes cooperation, synergy and collective progress, offers a framework for pursuing these priorities. Its credibility will ultimately rest on the government's ability to translate political commitments into measurable results. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Ethiopia's domestic progress also carries regional significance. As host of the African Union headquarters and a major political and economic actor in the Horn of Africa, the country has both a strategic interest in regional stability and an opportunity to contribute to it. A stronger Ethiopia, supported by trusted institutions and a resilient economy, would be better positioned to advance its national interests while promoting peace and cooperation across the region. Sovereign Sea Access: A Strategic National Priority For Ethiopia, access to the sea is more than a question of geography. It is closely connected to security, trade, economic competitiveness, national development and long-term strategic interests. Dependence on external maritime corridors exposes the country's economy to transport costs, logistical bottlenecks and disruptions in international trade. Reliable and diversified access to maritime infrastructure could help Ethiopian businesses reach international markets more efficiently, strengthen supply chains and improve the competitiveness of exports. Ethiopia must be an integral part of the Red Sea security architecture. As a major regional actor with longstanding contributions to peacekeeping under the United Nations and peace and security efforts across the Horn of Africa, Ethiopia has a compelling strategic interest in the security of this vital maritime corridor and a meaningful contribution to make. Excluding a country of Ethiopia's regional significance from decisions affecting Red Sea security would leave a critical stakeholder outside a process with direct implications for its economic and national interests. Ethiopia should therefore have a meaningful seat at the table, enabling it to contribute to maritime security, protect international shipping, strengthen regional stability and help safeguard one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Ultimately, the measure of progress will be whether Ethiopia can expand its maritime options, reduce trade constraints and strengthen its economic resilience while contributing to stability across the Horn of Africa. National Unity as Foundation of Strategic Ambition No national ambition can be sustained without internal stability and a shared sense of purpose. Ethiopia's new political chapter must therefore begin with the responsibility to strengthen national unity, address longstanding grievances and rebuild public confidence. The country's cultural diversity, complex history and competing political interests make inclusive state building essential. Unity cannot be achieved through declarations alone. It requires equal citizenship, constitutional protection, fair access to opportunities and institutions capable of managing disagreements peacefully. The Medemer approach can help create common ground among political parties, government institutions, civil society organizations, religious institutions, traditional leaders and communities. The national dialogue process offers an opportunity to address historical grievances, identify shared interests and build a stronger foundation for consensus. For this process to succeed, participation must be meaningful, diverse perspectives must be heard, and recommendations must inform practical reforms. National reconciliation should not be reduced to a political slogan; it must produce greater trust, improved relations among communities and more effective mechanisms for resolving disputes. Democratic Institutions: Turning the Mandate into Public Trust The durability of Ethiopia's political transition will depend heavily on the performance of its democratic institutions. Parliament, the judiciary, electoral bodies and executive institutions must operate within their constitutional mandates and provide effective mechanisms for accountability. The House of Peoples' Representatives has a responsibility not only to enact legislation but also to scrutinize government performance, examine public expenditure and ensure that national policies respond to citizens' needs. Effective parliamentary oversight can help identify implementation gaps, improve public spending and strengthen accountability. An independent and accessible judiciary is equally important. Citizens must be able to seek remedies when their rights are violated, while disputes should be resolved through impartial legal procedures. Consistent application of the law would reinforce equal protection and improve confidence in public institutions. Political parties also have a responsibility to strengthen democratic practices by presenting credible policy alternatives, engaging in constructive debate and respecting constitutional procedures. The government, in turn, must protect lawful political participation, civic engagement and public criticism. Combating corruption, reducing administrative inefficiency and improving public services are equally important. Transparent procurement, responsible financial management and accessible complaint mechanisms would help ensure that public resources serve their intended purposes. These reforms are directly connected to Ethiopia's broader strategic ambitions. Predictable institutions and accountable governance can strengthen investor confidence, improve the business environment and support the effective implementation of infrastructure and development projects. A government that earns public trust at home is also better positioned to build credible partnerships abroad. Democratic accountability is therefore not separate from national strategy; it is one of the foundations on which sustainable national progress depends. Economic Transformation and Building the Capacity for Sovereignty Ethiopia's pursuit of sea access must be supported by an economy capable of turning improved connectivity into prosperity. Access to ports and international markets can create opportunities, but the benefits will depend on domestic productivity, competitive industries and the capacity to generate value. In this regard, Ethiopia's "Made in Ethiopia" industrial movement is playing an important role in strengthening domestic production, advancing import substitution and expanding the country's manufacturing capacity. By encouraging local industries to produce goods previously sourced from abroad, the initiative supports economic self-reliance, reduces import dependence and creates opportunities for domestic investment and job creation. Agriculture remains central to Ethiopia's food security and economy. Under the Medemer philosophy, the country has made notable progress, particularly in wheat production. Expanding irrigation, mechanization, research and agro-processing can further boost productivity, reduce climate vulnerability and increase farmers' incomes. Industrialization, manufacturing and digital transformation are equally vital to diversifying exports, creating jobs and strengthening domestic production. Reliable power, efficient logistics, access to finance and a skilled workforce will be essential to building competitive businesses. Improved maritime connectivity could lower trade barriers and connect Ethiopian producers to global markets, while stronger domestic industries would help the country capture greater value from international trade. Horn of Africa and Red Sea Region Cooperation for Shared Prosperity Ethiopia's national future is closely connected to developments across the Horn of Africa. Conflict, displacement, food insecurity and climate pressures frequently cross borders, while political tensions can disrupt trade and threaten the livelihoods of border communities. The pursuit of sea access must therefore be approached within a wider framework of regional cooperation. Ethiopia's strategic and economic interests must be connected to the Red Sea coast in the near future for mutual benefits. Port operations, transport corridors, logistics services and cross-border infrastructure can create commercial opportunities for participating countries. Improved connectivity can strengthen regional supply chains, expand markets and encourage investment in transport, manufacturing and trade-related services. A more stable and connected Horn of Africa would benefit Ethiopia's maritime aspirations while supporting the development priorities of its neighbors. Ethiopia's regional influence will therefore depend not only on the scale of its ambitions but also on its ability to build trust, sustain dialogue and demonstrate that cooperation can deliver tangible benefits. Climate Resilience and Water Security on Nile River Equally important to Ethiopia's ambition for sovereign sea access, the new Medemer Government must maximize the development potential of the Abay (Blue Nile) River by advancing additional hydropower and irrigation projects. Harnessing this strategic resource is vital to expanding electricity generation, strengthening food security and accelerating economic transformation. Climate resilience remains central to this ambition. Droughts, floods and shifting rainfall patterns threaten agriculture, water supplies, infrastructure and livelihoods across the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia's investment in hydropower and irrigation must therefore go hand in hand with sustainable water management, environmental protection and climate adaptation. For Ethiopia, maximizing the Abay River's potential is not merely an energy or irrigation priority; it is a strategic pillar of economic sovereignty, food security and long-term national development. Youth and Women: Expanding the Foundations of National Progress Ethiopia's young population represents a major opportunity for economic growth, innovation and national renewal. Realizing this potential requires more than expanding education; it demands relevant skills, productive employment, entrepreneurship and meaningful participation in public life. Limited employment opportunities can deepen frustration, particularly when young people feel excluded from decisions affecting their future. Investment in technical and vocational education, digital skills and employment-intensive sectors would help connect education with the needs of the economy. Stronger links between schools, universities, training institutions and employers could improve the transition from education to employment. Support for entrepreneurship and small businesses could also enable young people to turn their skills and ideas into productive economic activity. Youth participation is equally important in national reconciliation, community development and public debate. Providing meaningful opportunities for young people to contribute to public affairs would strengthen social cohesion and ensure that national policies respond to their priorities. Women's participation is another essential component of inclusive development. Expanding access to education, employment, finance, public services and leadership would allow more citizens to contribute to national progress and strengthen household welfare. These investments have strategic significance. A skilled, productive and economically empowered population would strengthen domestic industries, improve export competitiveness and help Ethiopia benefit from expanded regional and international trade. National ambition becomes more sustainable when citizens have a genuine stake in its realization. Empowering young people and women is therefore not simply a social objective; it is an investment in Ethiopia's productive capacity, stability and long-term prosperity. From National Ambition to Measurable Results The credibility of Ethiopia's new political chapter will ultimately depend on implementation. The government must translate its priorities into clear targets, allocate resources according to national needs and establish mechanisms for assessing progress. Security, employment, public service delivery, institutional accountability and economic resilience should be central measures of performance. Federal and regional authorities must coordinate their responsibilities while respecting constitutional mandates and local circumstances. Consultation with communities, businesses, professional associations and civil society can improve decision-making and help identify emerging problems. Efficient public financial management, stronger procurement systems and effective anti-corruption measures would help ensure that limited resources deliver meaningful results. The government must also balance long-term infrastructure investments with immediate public needs. Citizens expect improved access to health care, education, affordable food, employment and personal security. Progress in these areas will shape public confidence in the administration. Strategic ambitions and domestic responsibilities should reinforce each other. Maritime access can expand economic opportunities and its full value should depend on productive industries, capable institutions, skilled workers and a stable political environment. The ultimate test is whether national policies improve the lives of citizens while strengthening Ethiopia's ability to pursue its interests through peaceful and constructive engagement. All in all, Ethiopia's new five-year political chapter presents an opportunity to strengthen the foundations of a peaceful, democratic and prosperous state. Its success will depend on the government's ability to translate its electoral mandate and the Medemer philosophy into tangible progress in national unity, security, institutional accountability and living standards. At the heart of the country's strategic ambition is sovereign access to the sea. Pursued through mutually beneficial arrangements, maritime connectivity could help ease trade constraints, strengthen export competitiveness and deepen regional economic integration as well as ensure lasting peace. Beyond its borders, Ethiopia must strengthen constructive relations with neighboring states, advance cooperation on trade, infrastructure, energy and climate resilience, and support regional efforts to prevent conflict. Its engagement with the African Union and IGAD can help advance these goals when backed by consistent diplomacy and practical commitments. The government's responsibility is therefore both national and regional: to build a state that citizens trust, an economy that expands opportunities and a foreign policy that advances national interests while respecting the legitimate interests of others. Sovereign access to the sea may be at the heart of Ethiopia's national ambition, but national unity, democratic governance and economic transformation will determine its success. The defining measure of the Medemer State will be its ability to turn this ambition into lasting improvements in citizens' lives while contributing to a more peaceful, stable and economically integrated Horn of Africa. The Medemer Government aims to enhance citizens' lives while strengthening Ethiopia's strategic position in the Horn of Africa. Access to maritime trade is essential for improving export competitiveness and attracting investment. The government emphasizes national unity, democratic institutions, and economic transformation as foundational elements for this ambition. Key initiatives include boosting domestic production through the "Made in Ethiopia" movement and advancing agricultural productivity. Regional cooperation is also highlighted, as Ethiopia seeks to connect its interests with those of neighboring countries. Additionally, the government plans to maximize the potential of the Abay River for hydropower and irrigation, addressing climate resilience and food security. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Seeking Renewable Energy Investment, Stronger Public-Private Partnerships
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Seeking Renewable Energy Investment, Stronger Public-Private Partnerships - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Seeking Renewable Energy Investment, Stronger Public-Private Partnerships 15 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia is seeking increased investment and stronger public-private partnerships to expand renewable energy use and support agricultural productivity, business growth and improved livelihoods. The ongoing Second Ethiopian Renewable Energy Summit 2026 which opened today focuses on attracting investment, expanding energy access and strengthening the contribution of renewable energy to the country's economic development. Water and Energy Minister Habtamu Iteffa, through his representative, noted that electric power is essential for economic transformation, industrial development, public services, agricultural productivity and improved living standards. Therefore, Ethiopia needs to expand its national grid while complementing it with decentralized renewable energy solutions, including solar home systems, mini-grids and technologies that enable businesses and communities to use energy productively. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "Our objective must be to move from dialogue to investments, from isolated initiatives to scale-up solutions, and from commitments to implementation," he said. The Minister also underscored the importance of private-sector participation in the energy transition through capital investment, technical expertise, innovation, distribution networks, job creation and local manufacturing. He said expanding the market requires a predictable policy and regulatory environment, access to finance and foreign exchange, quality standards and business models that make renewable energy solutions affordable and sustainable. Agriculture Minister Addisu Arega, through his representative, highlighted the role of renewable energy in improving agricultural production, addressing climate-related challenges and strengthening farmers' resilience to irregular rainfall and rising production costs. He said solar-powered irrigation can improve farmers' access to water, reduce dependence on diesel-powered pumps and support crop diversification. Renewable energy can also power cold storage, refrigerated transport and other facilities that help preserve agricultural products and reduce post-harvest losses. Moreover, renewable energy can support agricultural processing, dairy production, rural water supply, veterinary services, digital agriculture and access to agricultural inputs. However, high upfront costs, limited access to affordable finance, gaps in technical skills and challenges in equipment maintenance remain barriers to wider adoption. For her part, Ethiopian Solar Energy Development Association (ESEDA) General Manager Yemissirach Sisay said the summit seeks to demonstrate the readiness and capacity of private companies to contribute to Ethiopia's energy transition and turn the country's renewable energy potential into practical results. "The private sector is not waiting on the sidelines of national development," she noted. The General Manager highlighted opportunities in solar-powered water pumps for smallholder farmers, mini-grids for communities without adequate electricity access, clean cooking technologies and sustainable electric mobility. Addressing investment risks, foreign exchange constraints, taxation and financing challenges would help local companies expand from small-scale distribution to larger renewable energy projects. Yemissirach also stressed the importance of cooperation among African renewable energy associations to share experience, improve regulatory coordination, expand regional trade and support the development of a more integrated African energy market. The summit has brought together representatives of the government, renewable energy companies, private-sector investors, financial institutions, development partners and other stakeholders The summit, which runs up to 17 October 2026, provides a platform for collaboration and investment in the renewable energy sector. ethiopia.title: Egyptian Analyst Rebukes Egypt's Leaders for Trying to Block Ethiopia's Sovereign Right to Red Sea
ethiopia.content: Egyptian Analyst Rebukes Egypt's Leaders for Trying to Block Ethiopia's Sovereign Right to Red Sea - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Egyptian Analyst Rebukes Egypt's Leaders for Trying to Block Ethiopia's Sovereign Right to Red Sea 15 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — The Egyptian political analyst Magdi Khalil has strongly criticized the leaders of Egypt for opposing and fighting Ethiopia's right of access to the Red Sea. "If there were leaders in Egypt with vision and foresight, they would work to help Ethiopia gain access to the Red Sea instead of opposing and fighting it," he said. The Egyptian analyst criticized the country's opposition to Ethiopia's efforts to secure access to the Red Sea and called on Egypt to reassess its policy toward Ethiopia and shift from confrontation to cooperation. In a Zoom interview with ENA, Khalil said that Ethiopia, as a large landlocked country, has the sovereign right to gain access to the Red Sea. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "Ethiopia has the sovereign right to conclude agreements with countries to secure one or more outlets on the Red Sea, provided this is done peacefully, whether for fifty or one hundred years," he added. The analyst further questioned the reasons behind opposition to Ethiopia's access to the Red Sea, noting that Ethiopia's historical coastal presence had not been a source of harm to neighboring countries. Ethiopia's demands should therefore be addressed through cooperation and mutual interests rather than political confrontation and hostility. Khalil called for a meeting involving the countries bordering the Red Sea to discuss shared interests and reach regional understandings. The Egyptian analyst stressed the importance of replacing hostile competition with cooperation, emphasizing that peaceful agreements could provide a practical framework for addressing Ethiopia's maritime needs. According to him, some countries were willing to reach agreements with Ethiopia to provide maritime access, arguing that long-term arrangements could strengthen cooperation and stability in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region. Furthermore, Khalil criticized Egypt's historical position on the Eritrean issue, noting that Egypt, alongside other Arab countries, participated in supporting the Eritrean Liberation Front, which was established in Cairo in 1960. He argued that Eritrea's independence in 1991 and Ethiopia's subsequent landlocked status necessitate a reassessment of the regional positions that contributed to this situation. The analyst described Egypt's support for the Eritrean movement as a historical mistake that harmed relations that should have been based on cooperation between the two countries. ethiopia.title: Somaliland President Rejects Interference Threatening Ethiopia's Security
ethiopia.content: Somalia: Somaliland President Rejects Interference Threatening Ethiopia's Security - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Somalia: Somaliland President Rejects Interference Threatening Ethiopia's Security 15 October 2026 Horn Diplomat (Hargeisa) By Mohamed Duale Hargeisa — Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdillahi said on Thursday that Somaliland strongly opposed interference and any actions that could threaten neighbouring Ethiopia's stability and security. Speaking at the presidential palace in Hargeisa after returning from visits to the United States and the United Arab Emirates, Abdillahi, widely known as Irro, expressed firm support for Ethiopia's security. "We strongly oppose interference and any act that could endanger Ethiopia's stability and security," he said. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines His remarks followed diplomatic and military engagements between Somaliland and Ethiopia this week, alongside Somaliland's renewed willingness to discuss maritime access for its landlocked neighbour. Foreign Minister Abdirahman Dahir Adan Bakal said in an interview with Sky News Arabia , reported on Monday, that Somaliland was ready to discuss Ethiopian access to its coastline and Berbera port. He described Ethiopia as a close ally and urged dialogue to resolve regional disputes. Ethiopian Ambassador Teshome Shunde separately met Bakal and Somaliland army chief Brigadier General Nimcan Yusuf Gahnuug i n Hargeisa. According to statements from Somaliland's foreign ministry and military, the discussions covered bilateral relations, defence cooperation and regional security, with both sides emphasising cooperation to support peace and stability. Somaliland and Ethiopia maintain close ties spanning trade, security and diplomatic engagement. Their shared border and economic links make stability in the region an important interest for both sides. ethiopia.title: Can Ethiopia Ever Be At Peace? Four Reasons Conflict Keeps Flaring Up
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Can Ethiopia Ever Be At Peace? Four Reasons Conflict Keeps Flaring Up - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Can Ethiopia Ever Be At Peace? Four Reasons Conflict Keeps Flaring Up @TheVillaSomalia / X President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud (file photo). 15 October 2026 The Conversation Africa (Johannesburg) analysis By Alemayehu Fentaw Weldemariam Ethiopia has experienced recurrent conflicts for over five decades. This includes a long-running civil war sparked by the overthrow of Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974, renewed fighting in Tigray, and ongoing conflicts in Amhara and Oromia . The renewed hostilities in Tigray threaten to undo a peace process that had begun with an agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in 2022. Why has peace been so difficult to sustain in Ethiopia? My research on constitutional design and conflict points to four interconnected explanations: the foundations of the Ethiopian state remain contested ceasefires are mistaken for political settlements armed force continues to be a route to political power regional rivalries reinforce internal conflicts. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The problem isn't that Ethiopians of diverse ethnic backgrounds hate one another and can't live together peacefully. It's that successive political arrangements have failed to establish widely accepted rules for managing disagreements. 1. The foundations of the state remain contested Ethiopia's 1995 constitution emerged from a political transition that followed the overthrow of the military government in 1991. This ended nearly two decades of civil war . The new leadership sought to address long-standing grievances over ethnic marginalisation and demands for greater autonomy. It restructured the country as a federation largely organised around ethnolinguistic communities. The constitution vested sovereignty in Ethiopia's nations, nationalities and peoples. It guaranteed their right to self-determination, including secession . Proponents of federalism regard this right as protection against historical domination. Opponents argue that it entrenches ethnic boundaries and encourages competition over territory and resources . Ethnic diversity doesn't inevitably lead to violence. And federalism isn't inherently destabilising. It was introduced to accommodate competing national claims within a common political order. But constitutional recognition is not the same as political reconciliation. Read more: What is federalism? Why Ethiopia uses this system of government and why it's not perfect The problem arises when a constitution sets out rules for sharing power and governing the country without sufficient agreement among the political groups expected to follow them. Instead of providing a common framework for resolving disputes, those rules become another source of political conflict . 2. Ceasefires are mistaken for political settlements The 2022 Pretoria agreement was about stopping hostilities, not about resolving their causes. The federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front agreed to end two years of war. Major political questions were left for later negotiation. Disputed territories, regional administration, political participation and accountability for wartime abuses remain contentious . Eritrea, a major participant in the 2020-2022 war in Tigray, did not sign the agreement. Eritrean forces are still present in parts of Tigray. The Tigray People's Liberation Front itself also became fragmented after the war. Divisions emerged within the leadership. Disagreements over federal relations, political authority and control of military forces developed into a struggle within the movement. A peace agreement assumes that the parties signing it have authority over their political and military organisations to honour their commitments. But when these organisations fragment, it becomes unclear who can carry out agreements. The Tigray leadership's loss of legal party status in 2025 added another obstacle to political reintegration. These developments have undermined confidence that the transition from armed conflict to constitutional politics would be honoured. Read more: Ethiopia's peace deal is unravelling - what went wrong with the Tigray agreement This distinction is fundamental. A cessation of hostilities can save lives immediately. But it cannot, by itself, establish a legitimate regional government, resolve territorial claims or restore trust between former enemies. 3. Armed force is a route to political power The use of violence to acquire or retain political authority has deep roots in Ethiopia's modern history. In 1974 , the military overthrew the empire-state and established a military regime. This regime was itself overthrown in 1991 by a coalition of rebel forces led by the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front. These transitions reinforced a pattern in which political power could be won through armed struggle. When political opponents have little confidence that elections, courts or negotiations can bring change, taking up arms can appear more effective than peaceful political competition. The continued use of force by both the state and armed groups makes this cycle difficult to break . Read more: Ethiopia's national dialogue was meant to heal the nation, but divisions are deepening Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018 after years of anti-government protests and divisions within the ruling coalition. Two years later, rising political tensions led to war in Tigray. Abiy's regime has faced accusations of serious rights abuses and a lack of accountability. This has deepened distrust. It's made negotiated settlements harder to achieve. Under Abiy, political authority has become increasingly personalised. Military operations and extraordinary security measures have been used to confront political challenges. Peace needs a political environment where losing an election doesn't mean exclusion from power or exposure to coercion. 4. Regional rivalries reinforce internal conflicts Ethiopia's domestic conflicts are increasingly intersecting with the interests and actions of neighbouring countries. Eritrean forces fought beside Ethiopia's army in Tigray. They remained in parts of the region after the 2022 peace deal. Now the former allies are adversaries . There have been accusations of cross-border military intervention . This has renewed concerns that the war in Tigray could develop into a wider conflict. Ethiopia's ambitions to secure Red Sea access have further complicated relations with Eritrea and Somalia. Its 2024 agreement with Somaliland provoked a dispute with Mogadishu. Ethiopia also has strained relations with Egypt over its mega dam in the Nile River . Sudan's ongoing civil war and rival Saudi Arabia and Emirati relationships across the Red Sea add further pressures . Read more: Ethiopia and Eritrea are on edge again: what's behind the growing risk of war These external tensions can make domestic troubles harder to contain. Ethiopia has a duty to defend its boundaries and also to respect those of its neighbours. What would lasting peace require? These four obstacles to peace reinforce one another: disagreements over constitutional rules fuel political tensions armed conflict makes inclusive negotiations more difficult peace agreements that fail to address underlying grievances leave the door open to renewed violence competing regional interests complicate efforts to achieve lasting peace. As a result, Ethiopia's recurring conflicts cannot be resolved through ceasefires alone. Lasting peace requires all Ethiopians to agree on how power is shared, and the relationship between the federal government and its regions. Read more: What makes peace talks successful? The 4 factors that matter But resolving Ethiopia's internal divisions will not, on its own, settle tensions with neighbouring countries. That requires diplomacy built on respect for sovereignty, non-interference and peaceful negotiation over interests. Ethiopia therefore faces two interconnected challenges. First, building a political system that its diverse communities can accept. Second, establishing peaceful relations with its neighbours. Lasting peace depends on both. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia has faced persistent conflicts for over fifty years, including a civil war and ongoing violence in regions like Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia. Four main reasons contribute to the difficulty in achieving lasting peace: contested state foundations, misinterpretation of ceasefires as political settlements, reliance on armed force for political power, and regional rivalries exacerbating internal strife. The 1995 constitution, while aimed at addressing ethnic grievances, has failed to create a widely accepted framework for political reconciliation. The 2022 Pretoria agreement halted hostilities but left key political issues unresolved. Additionally, historical patterns of violence and external pressures from neighboring countries complicate the situation. Lasting peace in Ethiopia requires a consensus on power-sharing and improved diplomatic relations with its neighbors, addressing both internal divisions and external tensions.

ethiopia.title: Renewed Conflict in Tigray Raises Fears of a New Humanitarian Emergency
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Renewed Conflict in Tigray Raises Fears of a New Humanitarian Emergency - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Renewed Conflict in Tigray Raises Fears of a New Humanitarian Emergency Maria Gerth-Niculescu / Deutsche Welle Mekele in Tigray (file photo). 14 October 2026 Fides News Agency (Vatican) Adigrat — Nearly a month has passed since fighting resumed in Ethiopia, where an alliance of rebel groups led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) has launched a new offensive, reigniting a conflict that claimed hundreds of thousands of lives between 2020 and 2022. Almost four years after the Pretoria peace agreement was signed in November 2022 (see Fides, 3/11/2022), with the aim of ending the devastating war in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, renewed hostilities, reported in recent weeks, are escalating (see Fides, 30/9/2026). The Ethiopian federal army now controls much of eastern and central Tigray. According to local sources, government forces have also captured Zalambessa, a town of around 15,000 inhabitants on the Ethiopian side of the border with Eritrea. "As an ecclesial community, we are living under the weight of many pressures, tensions and anxieties. But, by the grace of God, we move forward. The situation does not look particularly promising. In our outposts, however, everything is under control, while sporadic gunfire has been reported in some towns." This is what a local source told Fides News Agency, requesting anonymity for security reasons. The renewed fighting is unfolding against a regional backdrop of increasingly tense relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea. After decades of conflict, the two countries signed a peace agreement in 2018. During the Tigray war, Eritrea supported the Ethiopian federal government against TPLF forces. Since then, however, relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated once again. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn One of the main sources of tension is Ethiopia's quest for access to the sea. Addis Ababa lost its direct access to the coast when Eritrea gained independence in 1993, after Ethiopia had enjoyed it for decades. The Ethiopian government regards regaining access to the sea as a strategic and vital national interest, while reiterating its intention to pursue this objective through dialogue and peaceful means. The geographical position of the two countries further heightens the significance of the dispute. Control of areas overlooking the Red Sea and the trade routes crossing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives the region considerable geopolitical importance. Beyond the renewed fighting, the humanitarian situation is a major cause for concern. Hundreds of thousands of people displaced from western Tigray have still been unable to return home, leaving around 44 per cent of the region's most fertile agricultural land inaccessible. In north-western, central and eastern areas where some farmers have managed to return, they have found farms and communities devastated by years of war. Adverse weather conditions have compounded the crisis. The first seasonal rains ended almost a month earlier than usual, compromising seed germination and causing crops to wither in numerous districts. The rains needed for the spring harvest, meanwhile, arrived more than five weeks late in eastern and southern areas, with some areas experiencing periods of drought lasting more than a month. The agricultural toll has been severe: more than 252,500 hectares of crops have been destroyed, while 140 districts are facing conditions described as catastrophic. More than 3.5 million livestock are also at risk of dying from hunger and disease following the disappearance of seasonal grazing lands and the depletion of groundwater reserves. The failure of the September harvest and the collapse in the livestock-to-cereal terms of trade have further exacerbated the crisis. According to the September humanitarian report issued by the Tigray Disaster Risk Management Commission (DRMC), 3.9 million people--more than half the region's population--were in immediate need of emergency food assistance. The threat of another famine is once again looming over Tigray. The situation was made even more desperate by events in Mekelle during the first weekend of October. As federal forces advanced towards the regional capital, coalition forces abandoned government buildings and police stations across the city. For around 24 hours, Mekelle was left in the grip of a serious power vacuum. Armed groups, reportedly made up largely of prisoners released after a nearby prison was abruptly abandoned, stormed and looted government buildings, post offices, art galleries and facilities providing assistance to the population. Particularly serious was the looting of infrastructure dedicated to the humanitarian response. Armed groups ransacked DRMC offices and warehouses belonging to the regional body responsible for coordinating relief operations and ensuring the provision of essential goods and services to the population. ethiopia.summary: Renewed conflict in Ethiopia's Tigray region has raised alarms about a potential humanitarian crisis, as fighting has resumed between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Ethiopian federal army. This resurgence comes nearly four years after a peace agreement aimed at ending a devastating war that resulted in significant loss of life. The Ethiopian government has regained control over key areas, including the town of Zalambessa, but the humanitarian situation remains dire. Over 3.9 million people in Tigray are in urgent need of food assistance, exacerbated by adverse weather conditions that have devastated agriculture. The recent violence has also led to looting of humanitarian infrastructure in Mekelle, further complicating relief efforts. The ongoing tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea add another layer of complexity to the situation, as both nations grapple with historical grievances and strategic interests.
